question:
Patient note:
A 41-year-old woman who ordinarily works as a middle-school physical-education instructor and runs half-marathons on weekends was transferred directly from the emergency department to the medical intensive care unit less than an hour after collapsing in her classroom with pleuritic chest pain, a dry cough that had worsened over three days, and a single episode of hemoptysis described by colleagues as no more than a teaspoon of bright blood. She has no prior history of chronic pulmonary, cardiovascular, hepatic, or renal disease, takes only an oral combined contraceptive for dysmenorrhea, and has never required hospitalization, systemic corticosteroids, chemotherapy, or other immune-modifying agents. She denies tobacco use, drinks wine socially once or twice per month, and has never used recreational substances. Family medical history is notable only for a father with hypertension in his late fifties; there is no diabetes, cystic fibrosis, or clotting disorder in first-degree relatives. According to emergency medical services, on arrival to the school she was seated on the gym floor, speaking in full sentences but reporting “sharp stitches” beneath the right scapula with every deep inspiration. Initial portable pulse oximetry on room air registered 88 % and improved to the low 90s after placement of a Venturi mask that respiratory therapy later confirmed was set at 38 % inspired oxygen; no intravenous fluids, analgesics, antibiotics, or bronchodilators were administered en route, and transport time was under ten minutes. Upon arrival to the resuscitation bay—and before any further interventions—the first documented vital signs showed an oral temperature of 38.8 °C, regular pulse of 99 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute with mild intercostal retractions, and non-invasive blood pressure of 116/71 mm Hg corroborated manually on a second reading. She was seated upright, speaking clearly, oriented to person, place, and date, able to recall three objects after five minutes, and followed multistep commands without hesitation, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 15 with no sedatives or intoxicants on board. Skin was warm and slightly diaphoretic with brisk capillary refill; there was no peripheral cyanosis, edema, or rash. Conjunctivae were injected, sclerae anicteric, and pupils equal and reactive. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated. Cardiac auscultation revealed a normal S1 and single physiologic S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and distal pulses were 2+ and symmetric. Breath sounds were diminished at the right posterior base with scattered fine crackles but no wheezes or bronchial breath sounds; percussion over that area was dull compared with the contralateral field. The remainder of the lung exam was clear, and tactile fremitus was increased over the involved segment. Abdomen was soft, nondistended, and mildly tender in the right upper quadrant on deep palpation, likely secondary to splinting; bowel sounds were present and normoactive. There was no costovertebral angle tenderness and no flank ecchymosis. Neurologic examination showed symmetrical strength and intact sensation in all extremities; coordination and gait could not be fully assessed given her monitored status. An arterial blood gas drawn within seven minutes of ICU bed placement while she remained on 38 % oxygen revealed pH 7.34, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 65 mm Hg, indicating moderate hypoxemia responsive to supplemental oxygen. Simultaneous serum chemistry panel demonstrated sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, chloride 104 mmol/L, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, glucose 102 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.46 mg/dL, the latter marginally above her last wellness-screening value of 0.9 mg/dL sixteen months earlier but still within laboratory reference limits and without accompanying oliguria, as Foley catheterization in the bay yielded 120 mL of clear yellow urine collected since her collapse. Complete blood count returned a white cell count of 12 600 /mm³ with 82 % neutrophils, hematocrit 38 %, hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, and platelets 245 000 /µL. Point-of-care lactate measured 1.6 mmol/L. Electrocardiography conducted concurrently showed normal sinus rhythm at 98 beats per minute with no ST-segment deviation or T-wave inversion. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained before initiation of antimicrobials or diuretics revealed a dense, wedge-shaped opacity in the lateral segment of the right lower lobe without air bronchograms, a normal cardiac silhouette, and no pleural effusion. Bedside bilateral lower-limb compression ultrasonography performed by emergency staff immediately afterward demonstrated a non-compressible popliteal vein on the right, raising concern for acute venous thromboembolism with pulmonary sequelae versus superimposed pneumonia. Focused cardiac ultrasound in the ICU showed normal biventricular size and function with no regional wall-motion abnormality and a collapsible inferior vena cava measuring 1.5 cm in diameter. No empiric anticoagulation, antibiotics, vasopressors, steroids, or intravenous fluids had yet been administered at the point these physiologic and laboratory data were finalized, ensuring that the recorded values—temperature 38.8 °C, heart rate 99 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 116/71 mm Hg, arterial pH 7.34, serum sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, creatinine 1.46 mg/dL, hematocrit 38 %, white blood cell count 12 600 /mm³, fraction of inspired oxygen 38 %, and PaO₂ 65 mm Hg—accurately reflect her untreated presentation at the moment of ICU admission for evaluation and management of suspected pulmonary infarction with secondary inflammatory response.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II sums acute physiology, age, and chronic health points. It ordinarily uses the worst values in the first 24 ICU hours; the available values give the admission score.
- Temperature 38.8 °C (38.5–38.9) → 1.
- Mean arterial pressure = (116 + 2 × 71)/3 = 86 mm Hg (70–109) → 0.
- Heart rate 99/min (70–109) → 0; respiratory rate 22/min (12–24) → 0.
- Oxygenation: FiO₂ 0.38 is below 0.50, so use PaO₂ rather than the alveolar–arterial gradient. PaO₂ 65 mm Hg (61–70) → 1.
- Arterial pH 7.34 (7.33–7.49) → 0; bicarbonate is not scored separately when arterial pH is available.
- Sodium 142 mmol/L (130–149) → 0; potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.4) → 0.
- Creatinine 1.46 mg/dL (below 1.5 and above 0.6) → 0.
- Hematocrit 38% (30–45.9) → 0; WBC 12.6 thousand/µL (3–14.9) → 0.
- Neurologic points = 15 − GCS = 15 − 15 = 0.
Acute physiology subtotal = 1 for temperature + 1 for oxygenation = 2. Age 41 (<45) → 0; no severe chronic organ insufficiency or immunocompromise → 0. Total = 2 + 0 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
